single_points.text: One reviewer states that enemies hit absurdly hard and can easily over fill your block meter.

citation.review_text:
Every time I thought about playing more, I thought about playing something better.

Valheim is deceptive in its appearance, it looks like norse fantasy survival crafting game, but it's actually a realism simulator with a norse fantasy coating, everything is realistic to the point of being a detriment.

[h2]Illusion of difficulty[/h2]
Enemies hit absurdly hard, as hard as you'd expect them to hit if they were real, it feels imbalanced just for the sake of realism.

You have a block button that also functions as a parry if done with exact timing, if you don't parry and block instead, you start to fill up the blocking meter, if it fills up all the way the damage from that attack goes through.
It seems like the game is balanced around parry, because as mentioned every enemy past the tutorial zone hits absurdly hard and will easily over fill your block meter.

After beating the first boss you can go to a new area, you need to go there to in order to begin progressing, but within it can spawn a miniboss that has half the health of the boss you just fought and [b]four times[/b] the damage.

[h2]Dying is tedious[/h2]
When you die, you drop everything you had in your inventory, including your equipped armor and weapons, and you lose 5% of experience across all your skills.
These penalties can be greatly reduced through world settings.

[h2]Collecting resources is slow and tedious[/h2]
Your maximum carry weight is 300, ore is extremely heavy and the first one you need weights 10 pounds, meaning you can only carry a total of 30 at a time, [b]but[/b] that's if you have nothing else at all in your inventory, so you'll actually carry around 20 at a time. Later ores weigh even more.

You can make a cart to put ore and other items in, but:[list]
[*]The more weight is in it, the harder it is to pull
[*]It obeys physics and can get stuck on terrain
[*]If left alone without you around, enemies will destroy it[/list]
It's just not worth using.

After copper, yo…

claims.claim: Reviewers report that inventory management is tedious due to weight limits and a lack of quality-of-life features like crafting directly from nearby chests.

citations.review_text: Whilst having a very strong early game, exploration and atmosphere, the further along you get the more frustrating the grind becomes and the severe, utter lack of quality of life features regarding crafting, ordering inventories, chests and other things made this game just annoying to play.

Valheim in my view is close to a master piece. No it's not perfect. The graphics aren't the best even if that was their artistic choice. I like the older look, but could you at least make it so things to mesh through each other? I always found that rather lazy. That being said, Valheim is such a delight to play. It's combat is simple and satisfying, and its roster of weapons is wide enough to keep combat interesting. Giving you good reason to use multiple rather than sticking to one type. It's Norse world is gripping, atmospheric and full of wonder. The game wants you to explore but you don't feel forced, you want to explore. There's always something new to find. The crafting is just as good, I like how crafting stations work and are upgraded, and I love how you discover new recipes as you find new resources. That being said, it was tedious having to  remove things from my chests when I often couldn't carry everything without being overencumbered, a simple mechanic where you can craft things that are in nearby chests would have been a big quality of life touch. But this isn't a big enough issue to make me dislike the crafting, it was still everything you could for in a game. Lastly, the boss fights, sailing, and meads are all what makes Valheim unique to other survival games for me. True many other survival games have bosses, but Valheim's bosses are utterly unique due to their setting. Meads are basically potions, but brewing them still felt different and I welcomed the change. Then the sailing. The sailing is scary at times, peaceful at times, and it opens up the vastness of Valheim's massive generated worlds. I don't want to spoil anything, but there's a lot to admire about this game. If you like boss hunting, crafting, base building (which is superb and due to its physics more thought provoking than other survival games, however more variety on building pieces would have been nice), and simple yet satisfying combat. You gotta try this game.

I'm surprised I hadn't reviewed the game yet. Anyhow, I enjoy the game quite a bit and would recommend people to give this a try, but some things to keep in mind. If you want the developer intended experience, sure, go on and play that, but if you want some very useful QoL features that "SHOULD" (aka they wouldn't make the game easier, just would make the game less tedious) be in the game in the first place, you need to use some mods for that. For example if you want seperate slots for your armor pieces to not take up precious inventory space, you need a mod for that; If you want nearby crafting stations to have access to materials in your chests, you need a mod for that etc. The game is fun, but combat can be clunky the first time. To me it still is kind of clunky but I'm getting used to it. The enemy variety is nice also. Another quick note, as a solo player, you may want to increase the Loot drop multiplier in the world settings a bit, otherwise the grind will be a slog, but if you already have plans immediately to play with friends, default settings are good for multiplayer.
Also unsurprisingly the game runs decently well. It has kind of a pixelated art style, which works really well and look gorgeous. Overall the game runs well, but even with my rig there is quite a few minor stutters and some fps drops here and there, and I'm not even exactly running the game at max settings, otherwise I'd have 100% GPU usage with heavy fps drops and stutters.
I got the game gifted to by an indie dev that I had by that time already helped test his game for a bit over an year as a thanks, and I'm happy I have been able to enjoy the game since around late 2024 or early 2025, I don't exactly remember.

claims.claim: Reviewers report that the survival systems rely heavily on timers tied to food buffs and the rested status, requiring regular maintenance to avoid severe combat disadvantages.

citations.review_text:
My friends and I have spent numerous hours playing since 1.0 dropped in September and we find many aspects of the game enjoyable! The enemy design, the bosses, the building, the environments are all unique and fun in their own way.

However, we have noticed while playing that for every enjoyable thing we come across, there is something else that leads us to question your judgement. For clarity, we are currently working on defeating the boss in the Ashlands.

For starters, the wind. It is interesting in concept, especially early game. However, when you force the players to sail in order to find new biomes, it gets to a point where it's just a tedious annoyance. And I know that the Moder buff forces it in your favor, but only for five minutes? With a twenty minute cooldown? Wouldn't that make more sense as a passive buff, a reward for slaying a dragon?

Also, why is the rested bonus so miserable? Having it enabled is absolutely necessary for any kind of combat and/or traversal, especially in the Mistlands. Yet it only lasts for 29 minutes at max level? Nobody is going back to their base every half hour.

Why is a crafting station required to build this late into the game? I understand late game constructions, but do we seriously need a crafting table to put a campfire down at this point? My suggestion is an upgraded hammer that allows the player to build simple wooden structures without one. Hell, we should be able to craft hammers that allow us to build anything without a crafting station.

On top of that, why can't we repair things without a crafting station? Even if it costs materials to fix things without one, we should be allowed to counteract the hundreds of vultures that decimate our boat's health while stuck on the Ashland spikes. The spikes that make it near impossible to traverse the waters in that massive boat that is also required to even enter the Ashlands.

By the way, vultures are scavengers; not predators. They should not be attacking us wh…

Valheim is a great game that's woefully held back by design that doesn't want you to play it.

At the core, the entire game runs on timers. You have three food slots that you must keep full, because you never upgrade your stamina and food. They only increase by eating food, and every biome has new food with better stats, and a slightly longer timer. If you die, all 3 food buffs disappear, and you need to eat more. Likewise, halfway through the timer, the food buffs start decreasing, so you don't even get the full value for the entirety of the timer. This is bad, because everything depends on your HP and stamina, such as your ability to dodge and block attacks.

Then there's the Rested buff. Rested is a near-mandatory buff for your stamina, without which you'll die quick. You get Rested by resting, in your base. Effectively this puts a timer on how long you're allowed to go out and hunt, explore, mine etc. A timer on how much you're allowed to explore, in an exploration focused game. This one also goes away when you die, meaning every death has you not just stock back up on food, but also sit around your base, before you can continue playing the game.

This comes to a finale with the bosses: You require all 4 of these timed buffs, all of which disappear on death. And a boss, naturally, will kill you a few times. So each death requires you go back to base, eat food, rest up for the stamina buff, then go back to the boss, grab your corpse, then spend time re-equipping your armor (because that's not instant, it has an interact bar), and only then can you continue the fight, if by then the boss or their minions haven't whittled down your HP.

All in all, I feel like the game punishes me for actually wanting to interact with the great biomes, crafting, combat (thanks for the dodge hotkey), and exploration. Which makes me not want to play the game, despite all of those aforementioned parts of the game being absolutely amazing. 

So if all of the above doesn't mat…

single_points.text: One reviewer says the performance in later biomes is terrible because destruction and simulated objects cause instability, and mentions multiplayer net-code issues with lagging enemy movement and unreadable boss animations.

citation.review_text:
This game is not ready to be called 1.0.
The performance in later biomes is terrible, certain enemies just create too much destruction and/or simulated objects to run stable. 
Playing this game in multiplayer comes with a terrible net-code, enemy movement lagging, where even the animations of bosses become unreadable if you are not the host for that fight. 
And the enemy health scaling when adventuring with friends just made the combat feel worse .

Doesn't help either, that the final boss soft-locked in his second phase, and getting the items to summon that boss again (without cheats) would take an hour, if not hours, of finding random Dungeons to then go to a random spot on the map for an invasion event.

cohorts.summary: Veterans navigate vast biomes while facing heavy resource grinds, late-game performance drops, and punishing death mechanics.

claims.claim: Reviewers report performance drops and lag in late-game biomes like Mistlands due to particle effects, spawns, and peer-to-peer multiplayer desync.

citations.review_text:
The game overall is great. Stylish graphics, simple but fun combat, and like most survival games, it's a really fun game to play with friends. The early to mid-game progression is peak, though across like five playthroughs, the devs' "anti-fun" or "anti-convenience" philosophy always drags down the late game:

- Bosses are mostly damage sponges with zero replay value. Once you get their one progression drop, there's no reason to fight them again, and even if you just want to refight one for fun or extra trophies, summoning gets ridiculously tedious by the end.
- Hitboxes are quite problematically thin/small. Standing on a teeny tiny slope makes you whiff completely with melee weapons on most if not all attacks.
- Even with the newly added extra inventory rows upgrades, late-game biomes can flood your inventory with random drops, and missing basic QoL like a crafting search bar or "quick stack to nearby chests" hurts.
- Dying nukes 5% (by default) of your skills that already take forever to grind. But honestly, skills barely impact gameplay past the early levels anyway, so there's little reason to stress over maxing them out.
- Performance tanks from Mistlands onward from all the particles/spawns, and if you are playing P2P with a friend, prepare for even more lag.

Still worth playing with friends. Just tweak the world modifiers or grab a few QoL mods so the endgame doesn't waste your time or kill your excitement.

One of the best Survival RPGs out there.
Just don't be irritated by the art style, if you give it a chance it can be very very fun and also rewarding.

Also the Game doesn't really throw information at you, so either find out the hard way, or go to the wiki.

I think this Game has so much to offer, but I'd like it to perform better with multiple Players. I hope they'll fix that in some way, in the future. 
Otherwise you can run it on a server too, but that doesn't negate the problem. Unless you have a ton of performance and connection speed, on everyone's single individual machine and the Server.
That's also where the problem lies, with PvP. The features are there, but the Game isn't build accordingly.
If one Player has bad Hardware or connection speed and loads an area (on a good Server), everyone in that area is affected by the first Player to load it. 
Not what you want, in a (mostly) parry-based combat System

Great first four biomes, terrible and unfinished endgame.

Valheim starts out amazing, but after the four biome, the game design completely falls apart—culminating in a rushed and frustrating Deep North expansion.

    Broken combat & hitboxes: Melee combat doesn't work on uneven terrain, and enemies like the Hex float out of reach while dodging slow ranged projectiles.

    Illogical progression: Crafting an ice staff from rare resources in an ice biome only to find out the local enemies are immune to frost makes zero sense.

    Artificial grind: Locking essential gear behind terrible RNG drop rates from frustrating enemies (like Hexes or 2-star Kriegers) isn't "hardcore"—it's just padding playtime.

    Unplayable multiplayer lag: The P2P netcode is a mess. Desync causes characters to get stuck on each other's heads at portals, leading to unfair deaths.

    Rushed atmosphere: Missing music and empty-feeling late-game zones make it clear the developers just wanted to push out 1.0 and be done with it.

Loved the early game, deeply disappointed by how the developers treated the rest of it.

still an early access game with bugs, terrible optimizaton in lategame, horrible netcode and just lack of proper QoL. Review would be positive if it was still an EA game, but it's supposedly not anymore.

Finally played through the game with a handful of friends on hardcore/modded and had a blast. But getting to Ashlands and Deep north had us all a bit frustrated. Felt rushed and ran really bad performance wise.

Up until Ashlands was an easy 10/10, but Ashlands/DeepNorth really dragged it down to a 7/10.

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the game features basic story elements, cutscenes upon defeating bosses, and an intricate random world generator with distinct biomes.

citations.review_text:
Valheim puts you in the pilot's seat of a Viking warrior sent to Norse purgatory. Fight, Craft, and Plot your path to Valhalla through immersive biomes, challenging boss fights, and the most intricate random world generator ever seen. 

Builders rejoice, hundreds of pieces with free build or snapping and Base defense events(optional).

Crafters and farmers, you'll find every weapon and armor set matters to somone's build, rewarding farming and cooking system with endless decoration possibilities.

Warriors, Rogues, and Mages, with a souls-lite combat system to fall in love with, I began to feel very comfortable with normal difficulty after early access ended. Then I tried Hard. Suddenly every second of food, every potion ingredient, and each kit upgrade mattered.

I've truly loved a few games in my 40+ years, but none will top this one for D͟e͟c͟a͟d͟e͟s͟ to come.

Valheim is a fine survival game. I wouldnt call it hardcore because only thing hard about it is how it trys your patience by throwing BS at you time to time. It's fun with friends and you can easily sink alot of time into it.

The story is very basic and serves its purpose as background noise sufficiently enough. Wish there was more to Thor and Odin beyond showing up every once and a while as terrain decorations.

itemgame is fine but there are alot of items that are underwhelming, Dev's trolling the players and flatout useless. The merchant materials which allow you to make unique weapons are rather underwhelming considering how tiny window of the game they are effective. The charms or relics effects are underwhelming considering how much you have to work for it to get activated. I like the Stamina and Tank armor builds but the Eitr armors feel underwhelming and I can hardly tell the eitr benefits with the armors.

the bosses the meat on the platter range from walking over them to actually engaging fights, the first boss is obviously easy because the game requires you to kill it early for progression. The Second boss doesnt exactly challenge you anymore beyond doing more damage but being less aggressive. but the remaining bosses are fun fights solo and with friends.

There are bugs, funny, annoying and gamebreaking which I think need to get fixed Like the final boss of the game stopping functioning in an immune state and you not being able to defeat them should not be there in the 1.0 update but yet it is.

Overall the game is enjoyable survival experience I recommend playing with friends.

One of the best survival co-ops I've player for the following reasons:
- Simple and yet stunning graphics 
- Game size is 4GB which is kind on storage
- The progression is rough at first but once you understand the game, it makes the risk worth the reward
- Every map is generated differently with all the biomes (no 2 play throughs will ever be the same, so great for replaying)
- The story feels epic now that there are cutscenes when you sleep between slaying world bosses
- I get to fish and farm when I want to choose 'cosy' instead of 'violence'
- I get to name pet chickens after people I know

Valheim has had an extremely long period of early access and I held off playing it until the full release so that I could experience the complete package from the developers. I definitely enjoyed my time playing Valheim and it is an excellent game to play with friends but I cannot, in good faith, recommend it to others in the current state. The game feels unfinished in so many areas that is really disappointing for a full release with such a lengthy early access. If the developers had over five years of early access and couldn't get a reasonable gear upgrade system in place I cannot recommend their game.

There were many good aspects to Valheim: I really liked the way the food system worked with it being one of the major factors to progressing in the game and having a variety of ways to access it (seeds to plant, animals to hunt or tame and farm, berries to forage), the food slowly degrading in stats over time - really strong system. I also loved the variety and creativity in the biomes and the way you had to get resources from them - sometimes you mine straight from the ground, sometimes you have to go into dungeons, sometimes you have to murder the local dwarves - and the logistics of moving these resources around was also a fun logistical puzzle. These elements also all involved a lot of exploration and the game excels in this area - exploring and finding new items, foods, ores, enemies, biomes etc. was very well done. The building in the game is rewarding but partly because of how awkward it is to build things. I liked the physics used in the game where you actually require proper support for your constructions but the actual building is cumbersome to use and lacks basic quality of life (QoL) features you'd expect to exist.

There are many systems which are clearly half-baked or tacked on and not in a fit state for a full release. Frankly I would be embarrassed to have released the game with the state of some of these. A minor but glaring example is the afor…

claims.claim: Reviewers point out that the game lacks basic quality-of-life features such as a crafting search bar or inventory management assistance like quick stacking into chests.

citations.review_text:
The game overall is great. Stylish graphics, simple but fun combat, and like most survival games, it's a really fun game to play with friends. The early to mid-game progression is peak, though across like five playthroughs, the devs' "anti-fun" or "anti-convenience" philosophy always drags down the late game:

- Bosses are mostly damage sponges with zero replay value. Once you get their one progression drop, there's no reason to fight them again, and even if you just want to refight one for fun or extra trophies, summoning gets ridiculously tedious by the end.
- Hitboxes are quite problematically thin/small. Standing on a teeny tiny slope makes you whiff completely with melee weapons on most if not all attacks.
- Even with the newly added extra inventory rows upgrades, late-game biomes can flood your inventory with random drops, and missing basic QoL like a crafting search bar or "quick stack to nearby chests" hurts.
- Dying nukes 5% (by default) of your skills that already take forever to grind. But honestly, skills barely impact gameplay past the early levels anyway, so there's little reason to stress over maxing them out.
- Performance tanks from Mistlands onward from all the particles/spawns, and if you are playing P2P with a friend, prepare for even more lag.

Still worth playing with friends. Just tweak the world modifiers or grab a few QoL mods so the endgame doesn't waste your time or kill your excitement.

I really like the game, I've put a lot of hours into it long before 1.0 and right after but I can't recommend it

It is fun and addictive but only in the very beginning. It gets stale, grindy and repetitive very quickly

My biggest gripe is that after so many years the game is missing SO MUCH QOL. You will constantly question yourself - is this really supposed to be this tedious? Yes. Is there a better way to do it? There isn't. I should be allowed to filter/search through my stuff... Yes, you should. Can you? No you cannot

Years of development time wasted, the game is dead - if you've played this during COVID - do not come back, it is not worth it

Valheim is not a bad game, it's quite good and is worth it's asking price but it does have some issues if you're thinking of getting it.

Valheim confuses excessive friction with difficulty. Things like dying can cause you to lose hours of progression just to get back to where you were, your mandatory food buffs degrade over time and last about half as long as they read, the entire fishing system is a clunky mess and for a game with this many items, crafting recipies and workstations there is no inventory management assistance, not even a search tool or the ability to lookup an item you've learned.

Valheim also comes with no detailed difficulty adjustment tools outside of some console commands to let players tailor the experience to their liking. If you're considering picking it up and and don't enjoy harcore-like mechanics (severe time and/or progression loss on death or making a mistake) I strongly recommend that you install a set of quality of life mods to help adjust the game to your liking.

Valheim has a unique atmosphere and a solid building system. But after five years of early access, 1.0 left me underwhelmed: the core problems are still there.

Grind. Every progression tier means hours of repetitive gathering. Ore can’t go through portals, so you keep making the same boat trips over and over. Yes, world modifiers exist, but I shouldn’t have to tweak a game’s settings to make it enjoyable.

Quality of life. Chests are tiny, and there’s no way to move items between them automatically. You spend ages sorting your inventory by hand. In 2026, that feels ancient.

Bugs. Water physics are sloppy: fish flying out of the water, desync in multiplayer… For a game that just left early access, that’s disappointing.

An underwhelming 1.0. To me, a new biome doesn’t make a finished game. Valheim feels as old-school and clunky as it did in 2021, only now it costs more.

Recommended if you want to build with friends, ideally with mods. Skip it if your playtime is limited.

- Hitboxes are quite problematically thin/small. Standing on a teeny tiny slope makes you whiff completely with melee weapons on most if not all attacks.
- Even with the newly added extra inventory rows upgrades, late-game biomes can flood your inventory with random drops, and missing basic QoL like a crafting search bar or "quick stack to nearby chests" hurts.
- Dying nukes 5% (by default) of your skills that already take forever to grind. But honestly, skills barely impact gameplay past the early levels anyway, so there's little reason to stress over maxing them out.
- Performance tanks from Mistlands onward from all the particles/spawns, and if you are playing P2P with a friend, prepare for even more lag.

Still worth playing with friends. Just tweak the world modifiers or grab a few QoL mods so the endgame doesn't waste your time or kill your excitement.

Great first four biomes, terrible and unfinished endgame.

Valheim starts out amazing, but after the four biome, the game design completely falls apart—culminating in a rushed and frustrating Deep North expansion.

    Broken combat & hitboxes: Melee combat doesn't work on uneven terrain, and enemies like the Hex float out of reach while dodging slow ranged projectiles.

    Illogical progression: Crafting an ice staff from rare resources in an ice biome only to find out the local enemies are immune to frost makes zero sense.

    Artificial grind: Locking essential gear behind terrible RNG drop rates from frustrating enemies (like Hexes or 2-star Kriegers) isn't "hardcore"—it's just padding playtime.

    Unplayable multiplayer lag: The P2P netcode is a mess. Desync causes characters to get stuck on each other's heads at portals, leading to unfair deaths.

    Rushed atmosphere: Missing music and empty-feeling late-game zones make it clear the developers just wanted to push out 1.0 and be done with it.

Loved the early game, deeply disappointed by how the developers treated the rest of it.

This isn’t a bad game, but the 1.0 release still hasn’t addressed most of the issues I hoped it would.

The early game is as great as ever and gets you hooked, but the longer you play, the more you start hating things the devs apparently consider features.

Combat isn’t great. Some weapons and builds are seriously underpowered or awkward to use, and fighting on slopes is still shit after five years, despite modders having fixed it long ago. Apparently, not being able to hit an enemy because they’re standing slightly uphill is part of the intended experience.

Valheim is sorely lacking in quality-of-life features, and players have been complaining about it for years. I honestly don’t understand why the devs seem so determined to keep basic conveniences out of the game.

The UI also feels extremely unpolished for a 1.0 release. I like the low-poly, retro look, but that doesn’t mean crafting and inventory management need to feel like they’re stuck in the ’90s too.

If you’re like me and play with mods, Valheim can be a great game and a lot of fun. But I can’t recommend a game that seems so committed to wasting my time for no good reason.

claims.claim: Reviewers note that the death penalty involves dropping all equipped items and a percentage of skills, making recovery extremely difficult when stranded far away without portals.

citations.review_text:
Valheim is a game with totally unforgivable game design mistakes and now outdated user experience. Notably, its death penalties are one of the worst I've ever seen, a true school-case of what NOT to do in game design. This alone prevents me from recommending it at all.

It's sad since the ambience and artstyle is nice, and it's one of the few viking themed games, moreover a coop one. But its issues are so heavy it drags the game right to the doorstep of hell.

[h1] What are the game's weaknesses? [/h1]

[h2] The death penalty mechanic is the worst I've seen [/h2]

Written shortly, dying actively tells you to stop playing this game.

In very hardcore games, dying usually means losing the resources and XP you earned thus far. Plus you have to redo some parts of the level. Difficult, punishing but fair : Each death is a new occasion to optimize your route, avoid traps you didn't see and learn the enemy moves. You improve despite your death.

In Valheim, each deaths makes your game insanely harder, a non-sense when you just faced a challenge too great for you. But how did they manage that? By making you drop all your items, including food, ARMOR AND WEAPONS. If you died while travelling on sea (there are sea and flying monsters) or if you didn't put a portal nearby, you'll have to build a new (expensive) ship and sail back there. And each time you die, you'll travel back with less equipment, sometimes to a point you'll just be naked on a raft that moves at a snail's pace.

And let's be clear, those food, armors and weapons are absolutely mandatory : Enemies will one-shot you while being near unkillable in the later parts if you are neither well-equiped nor well-fed. Also, in some biomes you will constantly take damage if you don't have the appropriate armor, making traversal almost impossible regardless of your skill level.

And the "best" part : Enemies will spawncamp your corpse. They can also spawncamp the portal if you died too close to it, leading to instant deaths…

Valheim is one of the better survival crafting games I've played over the years. It's slow, progressive and risky, in a good way. You start out with nothing, punching trees until it kills you, and by the time you're sailing across the ocean in a longship with a fully built base behind you, it feels like you earned all of it. Dying actually costs you, so every trip into a new biome feels tense. 

The building is great, the atmosphere is beautiful, and the exploration keeps you curious. Seeing new uncharted lands through the sunrise gives you moments most survival games just don't have.

It does need some quality of life improvements. The game also explains very little, which is good if you like that sort of approch. If you don't like a slow paced games or losing your gear, this probably won't be for you. But with updates, the game is becoming better.

Where Valheim really shines is with friends. Building a base together, splitting up jobs, getting wiped by a boss and laughing about it makes the whole experience far more enjoyable. Solo is still good, but with a group it's easily one of the best co-op survival games on PC.

Still getting killed by trees, still hating on the mistlands, still the death journey feel tedious, still the ore runs are harrowing. Still haven't cleared the mistlands :/

claims.claim: Reviewers describe resource gathering and transportation as a heavy grind, specifically highlighting heavy metal weight limits and the inability to transport ore through portals in vanilla play.

citations.review_text:
Want to have an adventure? Want a fair, challenging game where skill is tested? Want to explore and have a good time with your friends or family? Then welcome in Valheim! Where none of that exists.
Now, are you unemployed? have no life? like to play games as if it was a job itself? hate yourself? then this is the game for you!
You know a game is bad when most of the positive reviews are saying "mod this game" "good when you mod" but this review is for vanilla Valheim only, and not anyone else but the devs fixing the problems.
- GRIND: You go to an area, collect metal from nodes, and take them back home. Simple right? WRONG. Metal weighs crazy amounts so you can only carry so much on you before you move at a snails pace and draining stamina. Well there are carts right? so just fill the cart. WRONG. can't fill the cart too much or its too heavy to move. Its faster to be overweight, walk, drop items, wait for stamina, and pick back up for one trip then use the cart 3-4 times. This has taken HOURS to get a few stacks of copper and tin with two people. Also note, we had 2x drop rate so if you play how the devs consider "normal" then add double the amount of time. Now, this is just the black forest... it gets much much worse, why? because you can get to black forest with no boats, now think about this. The same thing as before in a new area plus having to boat to find the area to go to. Get the resources and then boat ALL the way back to your base. And if you just want to make a base at the swamp instead of bringing everything back? find another black forest and start all over again so you can make a forge to make everything else! or you know, you can just make metals go through portals which we ended up doing because we were having headaches just walking slow and sitting in boats for hours (which is normally turned off). Still on grind btw, items crafted take so many resources taking stacks of metals. 30-40 hours of work to make some but not all armor and a weapon or two…

Valheim has a unique atmosphere and a solid building system. But after five years of early access, 1.0 left me underwhelmed: the core problems are still there.

Grind. Every progression tier means hours of repetitive gathering. Ore can’t go through portals, so you keep making the same boat trips over and over. Yes, world modifiers exist, but I shouldn’t have to tweak a game’s settings to make it enjoyable.

Quality of life. Chests are tiny, and there’s no way to move items between them automatically. You spend ages sorting your inventory by hand. In 2026, that feels ancient.

Bugs. Water physics are sloppy: fish flying out of the water, desync in multiplayer… For a game that just left early access, that’s disappointing.

An underwhelming 1.0. To me, a new biome doesn’t make a finished game. Valheim feels as old-school and clunky as it did in 2021, only now it costs more.

Recommended if you want to build with friends, ideally with mods. Skip it if your playtime is limited.
